content: Apical vaginal prolapse refers to the descent of the uterus or the vaginal vault, particularly after a hysterectomy. Various surgical options exist for its management, but there is no consensus on the optimal approach. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of different surgical interventions for apical vaginal prolapse by comparing them against one another. The analysis included 59 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 6,705 women. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations such as imprecision, poor methodology, and inconsistency. 1. Vaginal Procedures vs. Sacral Colpopexy for Vault Prolapse: Women undergoing vaginal procedures were more likely to be aware of prolapse compared to those who had sacral colpopexy (risk ratio [RR] 2.31). If 8% of women are aware of prolapse after sacral colpopexy, this increases to 18% after vaginal procedures. Repeat surgery for prolapse was more common after vaginal procedures (RR 2.33). If 6% of women require repeat surgery after sacral colpopexy, this rises to 14% after vaginal procedures. Recurrent prolapse on examination was also more frequent after vaginal procedures (RR 1.87). If 18% of women experience recurrent prolapse after sacral colpopexy, this increases to 23%-47% after vaginal procedures. Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) was more common after vaginal procedures (RR 1.86). However, the effect of vaginal procedures on dyspareunia (pain during intercourse) was uncertain due to low-certainty evidence. 2. Vaginal Hysterectomy vs. Sacral Hysteropexy/Cervicopexy: There was little or no difference between the two groups in terms of awareness of prolapse, need for repeat surgery, or prolapse on examination. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was low to moderate. 3. Vaginal Hysteropexy vs. Sacral Hysteropexy/Cervicopexy: No significant differences were observed between the two groups for awareness of prolapse, need for repeat surgery, or prolapse on examination. The certainty of evidence was low to moderate. 4. Vaginal Hysterectomy vs. Vaginal Hysteropexy: There was little or no difference between the two groups in terms of awareness of prolapse, need for repeat surgery, or prolapse on examination. However, total vaginal length (TVL) was shorter after vaginal hysterectomy by an average of 0.89 cm. There were no significant differences in operating time, dyspareunia, or SUI. 5. Other Comparisons: No differences were found in primary outcomes between different types of vaginal native tissue repair, graft materials for vaginal support, pectopexy versus other apical suspensions, continuous versus interrupted sutures at sacral colpopexy, or absorbable versus permanent sutures at apical suspensions. Laparoscopic sacral colpopexy was associated with shorter hospital stays compared to the open approach and shorter operating times compared to the robotic approach. Transvaginal mesh did not provide any advantage over native tissue repair but was associated with a 17.5% rate of mesh exposure. Conclusions: Sacral colpopexy is associated with a lower risk of prolapse awareness, recurrent prolapse on examination, repeat surgery for prolapse, and postoperative SUI compared to vaginal procedures. The use of transvaginal mesh is not supported due to the lack of significant benefit and the risk of mesh exposure. There were no significant differences in primary outcomes between different routes of sacral colpopexy. Laparoscopic sacral colpopexy offers advantages in terms of shorter operating times and hospital stays compared to other approaches. No significant differences were found between vaginal hysteropexy and vaginal hysterectomy for uterine prolapse, nor between vaginal hysteropexy and abdominal hysteropexy/cervicopexy. The choice between absorbable and non-absorbable sutures did not significantly affect outcomes, but the evidence for mesh exposure and dyspareunia was of low certainty.
